title: Microstructured Optical Fiber Sensors: From Solid-Core to Hollow-Core Anti-Resonant Fiber Designs
content: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) sensing enables label-free, real-time detection for biomolecular, biochemical, and environmental monitoring. The integration of SPR with microstructured optical fibers (MOFs) overcomes the bulk and alignment constraints of prism-based configurations and opens a route toward compact lab-on-a-fiber platforms. This work thoroughly reviews the recent progress in MOF-SPR sensors and contrasts the performance limits of conventional solid-core designs with the emerging potential of hollow-core anti-resonant fibers (HC-ARFs). Particular attention is given to cladding engineering as a means of controlling phase matching and plasmonic excitation, which allows sensors to be tailored for refractive index, temperature, concentration, and analyte-specific detection. The interplay between waveguide geometry and plasmonic materials such as gold, silver, copper, aluminum, graphene, MXenes, and metamaterials is discussed as a key determinant of sensor response. Reported sensors are benchmarked in terms of sensitivity, resolution, figure of merit, and dynamic range across target classes that span gases, biochemical agents, proteins, and DNA. Finally, we outline the challenges and future directions toward low-loss, cost-effective, and application-specific MOF-SPR biosensors.
